chunks: "CMOS is efficient because in steady state there's no DC path from supply to ground: one transistor is always off. So power is only drawn when it switches.
The dominant term is dynamic power: each time the output goes low to high, the supply delivers C V DD squared of energy, half of it is stored on the load capacitor and half is burned in the PMOS.
On the way back down the stored half is burned in the NMOS.
So per full cycle you lose C V DD squared whatever the transistor resistance, and average power is alpha C V DD squared f .
So frequency matters linearly, and supply voltage and logic swing matter quadratically, which is why lowering V DD is so powerful.
If I halve the voltage I cut dynamic power by four. Rise and fall time don't change that dynamic term.
What they change is the short-circuit current: with slow input edges both the NMOS and PMOS conduct for a while and you get a through-current.
That's typically a few percent of the dynamic power if edges are fast and can reach 20% or more for sluggish edges.
Then there's leakage, which doesn't depend on frequency but grows with temperature and low thresholds. For example, a 10 picofarads load at 3.
3 volts toggling at 10 megahertz burns about 1. 1 milliwatts, and at 1. 8 volts about 0. 32 milliwatts."
